clinical_knowledge.topic: Invasive cervical carcinoma, locally advanced evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Invasive cervical carcinoma, locally advanced is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Refer immediately to Gynecologic Oncology, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: postcoital bleeding, foul-smelling watery vaginal discharge, and visible friable cervical lesion confirming cervical cancer

Key HPI features: 45F presents with 6-month history of spotting after sexual intercourse (postcoital bleeding), intermenstrual bleeding, and a persistent, foul-smelling, pink-to-watery vaginal discharge. Has not had a Pap smear or gynecological exam in 12 years. Complains of recent mild deep pelvic aching and pain radiating down her right leg.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 84, BP 130/82. Speculum examination reveals a 3.5 cm exophytic, cauliflower-like, ulcerated, friable mass replacing the anterior cervical lip that bleeds profusely upon contact with a cotton swab. Bimanual and rectovaginal examination under anesthesia demonstrates nodular tumor induration extending into the upper two-thirds of the vagina and laterally into the right parametrium up to but not fixed to the pelvic sidewall. Cervical punch biopsies confirm High-Grade Invasive Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the cervix (positive for High-Risk HPV type 16). Pelvic MRI and PET-CT confirm a 3.8 cm cervical tumor with parametrial invasion and two enlarged right external iliac lymph nodes (1.4 cm, hypermetabolic).
Relevant background/PMH: No regular medical care for 12 years, 20 pack-year smoking history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Invasive cervical carcinoma, locally advanced.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cervicitis/cervical infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Postcoital bleeding.
management_principles: Because the tumor extends into the parametrium and involves pelvic lymph nodes (FIGO Stage IIIC1 / > IB3), patient is NOT a candidate for primary surgical radical hysterectomy

Curative-intent treatment consists of Primary Definitive Chemoradiation Therapy: External Beam Radiation Therapy (EBRT) to pelvis combined with concurrent weekly cisplatin chemotherapy (radiosensitizer), followed by intracavitary brachytherapy boost to the cervical mass
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

learning_objectives: Identify clinical hallmarks of invasive cervical carcinoma (postcoital bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding, malodorous watery discharge, friable cervical mass)
Understand the role of human papillomavirus (specifically high-risk oncogenic genotypes HPV 16 and 18) in cervical carcinogenesis and the importance of routine cytology screening
Perform and interpret clinical FIGO staging parameters (specifically evaluating vaginal and parametrial extension on bimanual/rectovaginal exam)

Differentiate indications for primary surgery (Radical Hysterectomy for early Stage IA-IB2) vs primary Chemoradiotherapy (cisplatin plus EBRT and brachytherapy for locally advanced Stage IB3-IVA with parametrial or node involvement)

teaching.one_liner: 45F with 6 months of postcoital bleeding, foul discharge, and no Pap smear in 12 years — found to have a friable cervical lesion.

must_ask.say: Does the bleeding happen specifically after intercourse?
Can you describe the discharge — color, smell, consistency?
When was your last Pap smear or pelvic exam?

must_ask.objective: Screen for leg pain/swelling (nodal or nerve involvement)
must_ask.say: Have you had any pain or swelling going down your leg?
Do you currently smoke, and how much?
